concept.title: Metadata and social sharing
concept.shortdesc: Every page carries metadata in its head, read from the DITA: the tags that link previews, catalogues and search engines read. Nothing is invented; a value the DITA does not give is left out.

conbody.p: metadataOpen GraphDublin CoreWith the default govuk.metadata=basic, each page has Open Graph tags, which decide how a link to it looks when shared; Dublin Core tags, which government and library catalogues read; and links to its own address, its neighbours in reading order and its licence. govuk.metadata=full adds one schema.org JSON-LD block to each page. govuk.metadata=no writes none of them. The print document never carries any.

section.title: What each page carries, and where it comes from

row.entry: Tags
Read from
og:title, DC.title
The topic's title. On the home page, the map's title (a bookmap's mainbooktitle).
og:description, DC.description
The topic's shortdesc, else the shortdesc in its topicref. On the home page, the map's shortdesc or the bookmap's booktitlealt.
og:locale, DC.language
The topic's xml:lang, else the map's.
website on the home page, article elsewhere.
govuk.service.name, else the map's title.
The title of the top-level entry of the navigation the page is under.
The topic's category and keyword elements. A keyword that only repeats a word of the page's title is not a tag, and each tag is written once.
article:published_time, article:modified_time

The topic's own critdates, only when govuk.dates shows dates. Dates in a bookmap's bookmeta date the book: the toolkit copies them to every topic in place of the topic's own, so the plugin reads the topic's own from its source file, and a page with none has none.
govuk.organisation, else the bookmap's publisherinformation organization, else the bookowner organization.
The publishing organisation. With govuk.metadata.persons=yes, the topic's (or the bookmap's) author elements instead.
What the footer says: Crown copyright for official branding, else govuk.footer.licence, else the bookmap's bookrights.
The Open Government Licence for official branding, else govuk.licence.url.
link rel="canonical", og:url, link rel="prev" and "next"
The page's address, and its neighbours' in reading order, under govuk.site.url. Without it they are left out, since the plugin has no other way to know the site's address.
govuk.og.image: an absolute URL, or a path under the site root, which needs govuk.site.url.
Always summary; the other values are read from the Open Graph tags.

section.title: Structured data for search engines: govuk.metadata=full
section.p: JSON-LDschema.orgstructured dataAt full, each page also has one <script type="application/ld+json"> block in its head, in the schema.org vocabulary that search engines and language-model tools read. It is written from the same facts as the tags above, so the two always agree, and it adds the tags' structure: what the page is part of, and where it sits in the publication.

row.entry: On
The block holds
The home page
A WebSite: the publication's name, description and language, its address, and its publisher.
A topic page
A TechArticle: the headline, description, language, address, keywords, licence, dates when govuk.dates allows them, the publication it is part of, and the publisher.
A task page

The TechArticle also names a HowTo as its main entity: the task's title and description, and a HowToStep for each step, named by its cmd and told by its info (the command again when there is no information).
The landing page of a data asset declared a dataset

The TechArticle also names a Dataset as its main entity: the asset's name, description, address, licence, publisher, dates and version when it states them, its temporal coverage, and a DataDownload for each of its files. See . A standard or a service is not a dataset and gets none.
A glossary entry's page
The TechArticle also names a DefinedTerm as its main entity: the term, its definition, and its acronyms, abbreviations, short forms and synonyms as alternative names.
A generated page (glossary, index, lists)
A WebPage, with the same facts. On the glossary page, a DefinedTermSet of every term in the glossary is its main entity.
Every page below the home page
A BreadcrumbList: the publication, each page above this one in the map, then this page, numbered from 1. A heading in the map that is not a page is left out, so the list is always contiguous.

section.p: A Dataset is written only for a branch the map declares a dataset (a rdf:type of dcat:Dataset), on that branch's first page, with govuk.metadata=full. It does not need govuk.dcat. It is built from the same record as the catalogue record, so the two always say the same thing. For example, a branch that ships a table:
section.codeblock: <topicref href="topics/annual-return.dita"> <topicmeta> <data name="rdf:type" value="dcat:Dataset"/> <data name="dct:temporal" value="2025-04-01/2026-03-31"/> </topicmeta> <topicref href="data/annual-return.csv" format="csv" processing-role="resource-only"/> </topicref>
section.p: Two limits. A glossary of more than 500 terms has no DefinedTermSet: the glossary page already lists every term, and a block as large again would double it, so the set is left out whole (a partial set would be wrong) and the build says so (GOVK020W). And no search engine currently rewards HowTo: Google withdrew its how-to results in 2023. The block is written because it describes the page accurately for tools that read it, not for how a page appears in results.

The publisher is an Organization, or a GovernmentOrganization for the official and NHS brandings, named as govuk.organisation or the bookmap says. Every value comes from the same place as its tag, and a value the DITA does not give is left out. Without govuk.site.url there are no addresses, so there is no BreadcrumbList and no address in any object, and the rest is still written.

Values are escaped for JSON, and the characters <, > and & are written as escapes as well, so a title can never close the block it is in. A data block is not script, so a Content-Security-Policy (govuk.csp) does not restrict it; CI checks that in a browser. The block holds the headline and description a reader sees and nothing that is not on the page. To see how a search engine reads a page, use its structured-data testing tool on the published address. Which of the types a search engine rewards changes, so treat it as a description of the page, not as a way to change how it appears.

section.title: A catalogue record for data publications: govuk.dcat
section.p: DCATcatalogue recorddata.gov.ukA publication that documents data, such as a data dictionary or a data standard, can also describe that data to the catalogues that harvest it. With govuk.dcat=yes (and govuk.site.url) the build writes dcat.jsonld and dcat.ttl at the site root: the same DCAT 3 record in two serialisations, written from one graph so they are the same record. The home page links both and holds the record in its head. It is off by default, because a catalogue record is a publishing act, and the publisher turns it on.

The map says what is an asset. A branch of the map declares itself with a data element named rdf:type in the topicmeta of the topicref, topichead or topicgroup that heads it. The type is the publisher's statement and is never inferred.
section.codeblock: <topicref href="elements/index.dita"> <topicmeta> <data name="rdf:type" value="dct:Standard"/> <data name="dct:identifier" value="https://example.org/dictionary/elements"/> <data name="dct:conformsTo" value="https://example.org/model"/> </topicmeta> <!-- a distribution: a data file the site ships, inside the branch --> <topicref href="schemas/return.schema.json" format="json" processing-role="resource-only"/> </topicref>

ul.li: The type is a class of a vocabulary the plugin knows (dcat:Dataset, dcat:DataService, dct:Standard, adms:Asset) or an absolute address. One that is neither is reported (GOVK017W) and the entry is left out.

A submap is declared by wrapping its mapref in a topicgroup that carries the topicmeta. DITA-OT drops the topicmeta of the mapref itself, and of the submap file's root, when it resolves the reference.

The asset's landing page is its entry's first page. Its title and description are the entry's, else that page's. Its identifier is the address given as dct:identifier, else its landing page's address. The publisher, licence, language, rights and contact come from the publication unless the entry says otherwise. Any other property is a data element (dct:spatial, dct:temporal, dct:accrualPeriodicity, dcat:theme and so on) with the address or value the target catalogue expects.

A resource-only reference inside the branch to a file of a data type (JSON, CSV, Turtle, YAML, XML, a spreadsheet, a zip) is the asset's distribution. The build publishes the file at its path, and the record links it there with its media type and format.
One declared asset gives that asset, with no catalogue around it. Several give a catalogue of them. None gives no record, and the build says so (GOVK018W).
govuk.contact.email adds an organisational contact point. It is never a person by default.

section.p: A dictionary or a model: ADMS. A publication whose parts are not datasets, such as a data dictionary with a logical model and the specifications that conform to it, declares each part adms:Asset and says what kind it is with a dct:type address from the publisher's own list. The catalogue then holds each part as a member, typed adms:Asset and never a dataset, with what the map states: dct:conformsTo (a specification to its model, by the model's identifier), dct:references, and dct:isPartOf the catalogue. Give the model an identifier with dct:identifier so that every specification can point at it. A part that is retired, by importance="obsolete" on its first topic or a retired token on its outputclass, carries adms:status Withdrawn; state adms:status yourself to say something else: draft, completed or deprecated, or a status's address.

What data.gov.uk expects. A title, a description, a stable identifier and a licence. A record that lacks one is still written, and the build names the property and the record (GOVK019W), so the harvester will not be the first to say so.

Model honestly. A documentation site describes data; it is not the data. A data standard, a logical model or a data set specification is a dct:Standard. An interface is a dcat:DataService. Declare dcat:Dataset only for a branch that ships or links the data itself, and give it the files as distributions. A dictionary that holds many specifications is a catalogue of standards, not a dataset.

To check a built site, tools/check_metadata.py verifies the mandatory properties and that every reference in the record names a record in it, and tools/check_rdf.py parses both files with an independent RDF library and confirms they are the same graph.

section.title: Vocabularies for glossaries and code lists: govuk.skos
section.p: SKOSvocabularyglossaryas a vocabularyA glossary is a controlled list, and so is a code list. With govuk.skos=yes (and govuk.site.url) the build also writes each as a SKOS vocabulary that other systems can read: vocab/NAME.ttl and vocab/NAME.jsonld, the same vocabulary in two serialisations, written from one graph. It is off by default and independent of govuk.dcat: a glossary site wants vocabularies without declaring any asset.

row.entry: In the source
Published as
The glossary: every glossentry the map reaches
vocab/glossary, a scheme of all of them. The glossary page and the page of an entry that has one link it.
A glossgroup
vocab/NAME, named after the group's id, a scheme of its entries.
A subjectScheme map, referenced from the root map as a resource-only mapref

vocab/NAME, named after the map's id or file: each subjectdef with keys is a
concept, nested ones broader and narrower, and the top ones the scheme's top concepts.
A scheme the map declares: an entry, or the map itself, whose topicmeta (or bookmeta) has a data element named rdf:type with the value skos:ConceptScheme
vocab/NAME, named after the entry's first key, its id or its topic's file, or after the map's id or file: each topic beneath it that says it is a concept, with the hierarchy the topics state.

ul.li: A concept's label is the glossterm or navtitle, its definition the glossdef or shortdesc, its other names (acronyms, abbreviations, short forms, synonyms) are alternative labels, and a subject scheme's key is its notation. Text carries the language of what it labels.

A subjectdef that points at a topic with href is the concept that topic describes. What the entry does not say for itself it takes from the topic: the label from the title, the definition from the short description, and the keywords. So a concept that has a page is written once, in its topic, and the scheme map holds only its key, its href and its place in the hierarchy.

Keywords of a concept, in the subjectdef's topicmeta or else in its topic's prolog, are written as govuk.skos.keywords says: alt (the default) as alternative labels, for keywords that are the concept's other names; hidden as hidden labels, for keywords that are phrases people search with and not names; no not at all. A keyword that repeats the label, or another keyword, is left out.
A related-links link from one glossary entry to another is skos:related. A term marked retired (outputclass) carries its status.

relationship tablerelated conceptsRelated concepts of a subject scheme, or of a scheme the map declares, come from the map's relationship tables and from the topics' own links. A row of a reltable relates each concept in one cell to each in the others, whether the entry names the concept by keyref or by href; a related-links link an author writes from one concept's topic to another's relates the two. Both concepts then say skos:related. An entry or a link to something that is not a concept of the same scheme relates nothing, so the same table can still link concepts to ordinary pages for readers.

A concept's address is, in this order: one the source states (resourceid appid in the entry's prolog, or a data element named dct:identifier, on the subjectdef or in the topic it points at); the address of its page, if it has one; an anchor on the glossary page, which is given to every term for this; in a subject scheme, its key as a fragment of the vocabulary file. State the address a concept already has, so that links already made to it still mean it. The page it is described on is then linked from it. Two terms that state the same address are reported (GOVK021W); a subjectdef and the topic it points at are one concept, not two.

Changed in 1.5.0. A subjectdef whose href points at a page of the site now has the page's address, where 1.4 gave it its key in the vocabulary file; it takes its label from the topic's title where 1.4 used the key, when it has no navtitle; and its keywords are alternative labels. If others already cite the addresses a 1.4 build wrote, state them with dct:identifier before you upgrade, and they do not move.

Any other property is a data element: in a subjectdef's topicmeta or a glossary entry's prolog for a concept, and in the scheme map's own topicmeta or a glossgroup's prolog for a scheme. It is written when the SKOS table maps it: for a concept, dct:alternative (one more alternative label each time it is given); for a scheme, dct:description and dct:license, whose value is the licence's address. A misspelt name is reported (GOVK011W) and left out.

A concept's notes are data elements named for the SKOS note properties, each as often as it is needed: skos:scopeNote (what the concept covers and what it does not), skos:example, skos:note, skos:editorialNote (for those who maintain the vocabulary), skos:historyNote and skos:changeNote. A long note can be the element's content instead of its value.

The status of a concept or of a scheme is a data element named adms:status, whose value is draft, completed, deprecated or retired, written as the status of the ADMS vocabulary it stands for (under development, completed, deprecated, withdrawn), or the address of a status in another vocabulary. Only retired has another spelling (the outputclass), and only a retired topic is demoted in search.
A scheme's version and dates are data elements in the scheme map's topicmeta: dcat:version, dct:issued and dct:modified, the dates in ISO form (2026-11-02). A date that is not one is left out.
A publication with no glossary entry, no subject scheme and no declared scheme gets no vocabulary and a warning (GOVK022W).

section.p: vocabularyconcept topicsA concept system: each concept a topic with a page of its own. A glossary entry cannot hold a diagram, a table of associations or a discussion; a concept topic can. Say that a topic is a concept, and which scheme it is in, and the build publishes the scheme as a vocabulary like the others.
section.codeblock:
<!-- in the map: the entry that heads the concepts declares their scheme --> <topicref href="concepts/index.dita" keys="care"> <topicmeta> <data name="rdf:type" value="skos:ConceptScheme"/> <data name="dct:identifier" value="https://example.org/care/"/> </topicmeta> <topicref href="concepts/care_plan.dita"/> … </topicref>
<!-- in concepts/care_plan.dita: the topic says it is a concept, and what is broader --> <prolog> <metadata><keywords><keyword>Plan of care</keyword></keywords></metadata> <data name="rdf:type" value="skos:Concept"/> <data name="dct:identifier" value="https://example.org/care/care_plan"/> <data name="skos:broader" value="https://example.org/care/healthcare_activity"/> <data name="skos:exactMatch" value="https://other.example/concept/care_plan"/> </prolog>

ul.li: The scheme is the nearest entry above the topic, the topic's own entry included, that declares one; else the map, when its own topicmeta or a bookmap's bookmeta declares one. Its title and description are the entry's (for the map, the publication's, with its licence, edition and dates), its other properties are its data elements, its address is the dct:identifier it states or else vocab/NAME.ttl#scheme, and the page it is described on is linked from it. A topic that says it is a concept under no declared scheme is in no vocabulary, and the build says so (GOVK025W).

The concept has the topic's title as its label, its short description as its definition, its keywords as govuk.skos.keywords says, and its other properties (notes, status) from the data elements of its prolog. Its address is the one the topic states, else the address of its page. Only a topic that says so is a concept: the page that heads the scheme, and any other page beneath it, is not.

The hierarchy is what the topics state, not the nesting of the map, which is for reading: a concept is often placed under an overview page, or under a concept it is not a kind of. State skos:broader or skos:narrower with the other concept's address. Say it from either end: the vocabulary says it from both, and a concept with nothing broader is a top concept of the scheme. A scheme whose topics state no hierarchy is a flat list. A value that names no concept of the same scheme is left out and reported (GOVK026W).
skos:related is likewise said by both concepts when both are in the scheme, and written as stated when the other is not.

Alignment with another vocabulary is skos:exactMatch, skos:closeMatch, skos:broadMatch, skos:narrowMatch or skos:relatedMatch, whose value is the other vocabulary's address for its concept. They are written as stated, for a subjectdef and a glossary entry too.

The concept's page links the vocabulary's two files (rel="alternate"), as does the page of a concept a subjectdef points at. With govuk.metadata=full the page's structured data also says the page is about the concept (a DefinedTerm as its mainEntity, naming its scheme), with the concept's own address when the source states one. Neither is written without govuk.skos=yes.
Two vocabularies cannot have one file name. The first is written and the second reported (GOVK027W): give the scheme an id or keys of its own.
The same declaration makes the branch an asset of the catalogue record, when govuk.dcat=yes is set as well: a code list or a taxonomy is catalogued, and its concepts are published.

section.p: vocabularystable addressesKeep keys and addresses apart in a vocabulary that others will cite. A subjectdef's key is what authors write in keyref, and by default it is also the end of the concept's address (vocab/NAME.ttl#KEY). Renaming the key, the map or the site then moves the concept, and every link another system has made to it breaks. State the addresses instead: a data element named dct:identifier in the scheme map's own topicmeta for the scheme, and one in each subjectdef's topicmeta for its concept. Every reference to the scheme and its concepts then uses those addresses, and the key is written only as the concept's notation.

An address must be an absolute http, https or urn address, or it is ignored. Choose one you can keep: it need not be on this site, but a reader who follows it should reach something, so make it resolve when you can. A draft whose identifiers are provisional can leave them out and state them before the vocabulary is first cited.

vocabularyfinding the filesFinding the files. The home page links every vocabulary, in both forms, with rel="alternate" and the scheme's title; the glossary page and the page of each concept link the vocabulary that concept is in; and llms.txt lists them under Vocabularies, with a scheme's description. So a reader, a harvester or an agent that reaches any of those
finds the files. sitemap.xml does not list them: it is a list of pages.

PDFvocabulariesThe PDF does not include the vocabularies. The print document, and the PDF made from it, hold the publication's pages, with its title and author in the PDF's own properties. They hold no SKOS: the vocabulary files are not attached to the PDF and their addresses are not written into it, and the same is true of the catalogue record. A reader of the PDF who needs a vocabulary takes it from the site, at the addresses above, so give the site's address in the publication itself if the PDF will travel without it.

To check a built site, tools/check_metadata.py verifies that every reference in a vocabulary names a concept in it, that a hierarchy says the same thing from each end and that the home page links every vocabulary file, and tools/check_rdf.py parses both files with an independent RDF library and confirms they are the same graph.

section.title: Any other property: data elements
section.p: metadatadata elementA <data name="prefix:term" value="…"/> in a bookmap's bookmeta, the topicmeta of a map or an entry, or a topic's prolog states a property in a published vocabulary. The prefixes are dct (Dublin Core terms), dcat, adms, skos, rdf, foaf, org, vcard, schema and og.

ul.li: A property reaches every tag that is read from it. The example adds an article:tag.
A correct term that nothing at this level reads, such as dct:spatial, is kept for the catalogue outputs to come, and is not written.
A name that is not a term of those vocabularies, such as a misspelt dct:spacial, is reported once per build (GOVK011W) and left out.
A data element whose name has no prefix is the publisher's own, and is not metadata.

section.p: A page states its own properties first, from the entries above it in the map and then from its prolog. It takes the rest from the publication, except the properties that describe one thing only: its title, description, identifier, type, subjects and dates. A system that generates DITA should follow the guide for source systems.

section.title: Your own vocabulary and mapping tables
section.p: metadatayour own vocabularyvocabularynamed relationshipsThe plugin knows a fixed set of vocabularies, and its tables write a fixed set of properties. A publication with a vocabulary of its own, such as a concept system whose concepts are joined by named relationships ("an assessment precedes a plan"), names two files, and nothing in the plugin changes.

govuk.metadata.vocabularies names a file of vocabularies. Each has a prefix, a namespace and its terms; open="yes" in place of the terms accepts any term under the prefix. List the terms when you can: a misspelt one is then reported (GOVK011W) and not quietly written. A prefix the plugin already knows keeps its namespace and gains the terms you list.
A term of that vocabulary is then metadata wherever a data element is:

govuk.metadata.tables names a file of mapping tables, which say where a term is written. A table is a scheme; a file holds one, or a schemes element holding several. This one writes the two relationships as properties of a concept in the vocabulary files:
section.codeblock: <scheme id="relations" syntax="rdf" levels="skos"> <prefix name="ex" uri="https://example.org/def/relations#"/> <kind record="term"> <property term="ex:isProvidedWith" as="ex:isProvidedWith" format="uri" node="yes" repeat="yes"/> <property term="ex:precedes" as="ex:precedes" format="uri" node="yes" repeat="yes"/> </kind> </scheme>

ul.li: syntax is what the table writes: meta or link elements in a page's head, a json-ld block there, or rdf in the catalogue record and the vocabulary files.
levels is when it is on: basic and full are the levels of govuk.metadata, dcat is govuk.dcat=yes and skos is govuk.skos=yes. Left out, the table is on wherever its syntax is written.
A kind names the record its rows describe: a publication, a page, an asset, a scheme or a term.

A row reads the property named by term and writes it as as. format="uri" keeps only an absolute address, node="yes" writes it as a reference to a thing and not as text, repeat="yes" writes every value and not only the first, and lang="yes" gives text the language of what it describes.
Your tables are added after the plugin's own, so they add properties and cannot take any away. A prefix a table declares is written only in a file that uses it.
The plugin's own tables, in its resource/metadata folder, are the reference for the format: your tables are read exactly as they are.

section.p: A path is relative to the folder the build is run from. A file that holds no vocabulary, or no table, is reported (GOVK023W, GOVK024W) and the build goes on without it. The files are inputs to your build like your stylesheet: a table can write any tag into every page's head, so take one only from a source you trust.

What stays out is the ontology itself: the domain, range and multiplicity of a relationship. Publish that as a file of its own, declare it as a distribution of the catalogue record: the relationships the vocabulary files name are defined there.

section.title: Checking
section.p: A page the metadata tables require a value for, and that has none, is reported once per build for all such pages (GOVK012W). To look at a published page as a link preview will, use a social network's sharing debugger, or read the page's source. The repository's tools/check_metadata.py checks a built site against the same tables offline. It runs from wherever it is kept: it takes the tables from the plugin installed in the toolkit the dita command belongs to, from DITA_HOME, or from the toolkit named with --dita-dir; --tables names the plugin's resource/metadata folder directly. When it cannot find them it says where it looked and exits with status 2.

section.title: An index for language models: llms.txt
section.p: llms.txtlanguage modelsWhen govuk.site.url is set, the build writes llms.txt at the site root beside sitemap.xml. It follows the llms.txt convention: a short Markdown index that a language model, or an agent reading the site, can use instead of crawling it. govuk.llms=no turns it off.

It holds the publication's title and description, then a section for each top-level entry in the map, listing its pages with the titles and short descriptions the home page shows, each linked by its full address. The pages are the sitemap's: topics that are resource-only or toc="no", the search page and the print document are left out. With govuk.skos=yes the vocabulary files come next, under Vocabularies: the Turtle and the JSON-LD of each, by the scheme's title. The glossary, index and list pages come last, under Optional, which a reader short of room may skip.
section.codeblock:
# GOV.UK DITA plugin manual
> How to install and use org.istanduk.gov-uk, …
## Getting started
- [Installing the plugin](https://example.org/manual/topics/install.html): Install the plugin …
section.p: What it does and does not do. A minority of sites publish one, and as of October 2026 no major AI company says its systems read it; the main web crawlers rarely ask for it. The tools that do read it are mostly coding assistants and documentation tools that are pointed at a site. The plugin writes it because it costs nothing and lists only what the site already publishes, not because it is known to help.

robots.txtIf you do not want your content used to train AI models, llms.txt is the wrong tool: leaving it out does not keep a site out of training data, and publishing it gives no permission. Set Disallow rules in robots.txt for the crawlers you want to exclude (each AI company documents its crawler's name), and say what reuse you allow in your licence. The robots.txt the plugin writes beside the sitemap allows every crawler; ship your own in the output folder and the plugin leaves it alone.

The convention also suggests a Markdown copy of every page, and a full-text llms-full.txt. The plugin writes neither: its pages are HTML, and the print document already holds the whole publication. A separate toolkit plugin, fox.jason.llms.txt, makes Markdown output if you need it.
